To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effect of residual lignin on cellulose hydrolytic activity of cellulase enzymes is due to a combination of physical hindrance and non-productive binding of cellulolytic enzymes to lignin, and that cold alkali treatment selectively reduces the lignin component that has a high affinity for protein.
(a) the residual lignin in steam-exploded softwood has a high affinity for protein and that (b) this lignin fraction can be removed by mild alkali treatment.
the residual lignin in pretreated Douglas-fir is heterogeneous and can be separated into fractions of different affinity for cellulase proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of pretreatments that are more efficient and less expensive.
the effects of residual lignin on cellulose hydrolytic enzymes and how these effects can be minimized by pretreatment of biomass with alkali.
the development of pretreatment technologies that will allow lignocellulosic biomass to be converted to fermentable sugars at a competitive price with respect to starch and sugar.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of residual lignin in steam-exploded softwood can be reduced by alkali extraction and that this lignin is not removed by alkali extraction from organosolv pretreated softwood.
lignin is a major inhibitor of enzymatic cellulose hydrolyses, and that the most effective means to overcome this inhibition is to minimize the amount of lignin in the substrate.
lignin is a complex and heterogeneous material, and its effects on enzymatic hydrolysation of pretreated lignocellulosic substrates are complex and variable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lignin in the pretreated softwood substrates studied here can be divided into three fractions.
lignin reduction by cold alkali is not a viable strategy for enhancing enzymatic hydrolyse of softwoods, but that protein addition is a promising approach.
the effect of residual lignin on cellulose hydrolytic activity is complex and depends on the lignin content and the method used to remove it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the residual lignin content of the pretreated feedstock is not a good predictor of the extent to which it can be converted into fermentable sugars by cellulolytic enzyme hydrolysis.
the lignin remaining in pretreated lignocellulose can have a profound impact on cellulose hydrolytic efficiency.
the effect of residual lignin on cellulose hydrolytic conversion can be reduced, but not eliminated by mild alkali extraction.
